description: Hi! I'm interested in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, especially the Earth Information Jukebox challenge. I'm a programming beginner passionate about music, sound design, and creativity. I'm looking for teammates skilled in coding, data, or app development. I'm eager to learn and contribute creatively. If you're interested, let's team up!
summary:
Our challenge was to utilize NASA's satellite images and convert them into audio. Our core feature is providing access to NASA's data, which is available as static numbers or images, through a process called sonification. Our target audience is visually impaired individuals. To support this group, we have included a Personal Assistant (PA) to guide users throughout their experience.

This initiative creates a meaningful impact by helping visually impaired people become more independent and access information of interest through an accessible website. It not only presents data in an engaging way but also fosters an enthusiastic experience, allowing users to "feel the Earth." Furthermore, it helps users plan their day according to their preferences, as they can now truly FEEL the weather for the day.
details:
Earth Information Jukebox lets anyone hear Earth science. Ask by typing or talking, for example "rain in Kathmandu" or "global temperature." The app answers with real NASA data in three ways: a NASA Earth Information Center visualization on screen, a live soundscape driven by the data, and a voice that explains the result in plain language.

How it works: For any place you name, the app gets the latitude and longitude and pulls daily rainfall and temperature from the NASA POWER API. Rain intensity drives the sound, and dry days play a calm cue instead of fake rain. Global temperature comes from NASA GISTEMP v4 and plays as a tone that rises with warming. Visuals come from NASA SVS EIC imagery. Google Gemini only narrates; NASA data is always the source of truth.

Impact: Sound and speech open climate data to people who are blind or have low vision, people who don't read charts, and people who don't speak English. Replies can be spoken in Nepali, Hindi, Japanese and more. Our motivating example is monsoon awareness in Kathmandu.

Tools: JavaScript, Node.js/Express, Web Audio API, Web Speech API, Google Gemini (chat, Live voice, text-to-speech), NASA POWER, GISTEMP and SVS, hosted on Render.

Creativity and considerations: It's a jukebox for the planet: say "Hey Jukebox," ask about anywhere on Earth, and interrupt it mid-answer. We focused on honest sound (no invented rain), accessibility (voice-first, keyboard shortcuts), privacy (the wake word is off by default), and reliability (it falls back to NASA-only answers if the AI service is busy).
